conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: InitialStopBeyondSignalBar
candidates.quote: The initial price action stop for most trades is one tick beyond the signal bar until the entry bar closes, when it is tightened to one or two ticks beyond the entry bar if the entry bar is strong.
candidates.description: The initial protective stop for a long is placed one tick below the low of the signal bar (the bar whose close triggered the entry); for a short, one tick above its high. It stays in force until the entry bar closes.
candidates.pseudocode:
signalBarLow = low[ctx.BarsSinceEntry() + 1]; // the bar immediately before the entry bar -- still the signal bar while the entry bar has not yet closed
exitLongStop = ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && low[0] <= signalBarLow - stopOffsetTicks * tick;
candidates.book_order_type: protective sell stop one tick below the signal bar's low (buy stop above its high for shorts)

complexity.reason: the signal bar has to be located dynamically via BarsSinceEntry() rather than a fixed lag, since the offset into history grows every bar the trade stays open

notes: Foundational stop for the whole chapter; nearly every other exit candidate here modifies or replaces this one.
Distinct from the corpus's dollar-based StopLoss: this is a price-action stop tied to a specific bar, not a fixed dollar amount.

candidates.name: EntryBarIsStrongTrendBar
candidates.quote: If the entry bar is a doji, then rely on your original stop.
candidates.description: Shared primitive for this chapter: once the entry bar (the bar immediately following the signal bar, during which the position was filled) closes, classify it as a strong trend bar if its body is a large fraction of its range and closed in the trade's direction. Used to gate whether the stop tightens (R29-03).
candidates.pseudocode: entryBarLow = low[ctx.BarsSinceEntry()]; entryBarHigh = high[ctx.BarsSinceEntry()]; entryBarBody = close[ctx.BarsSinceEntry()] - open[ctx.BarsSinceEntry()]; entryBarRange = entryBarHigh - entryBarLow; isEntryBarStrongTrendBar = ctx.BarsSinceEntry() >= 1 && entryBarBody > 0 && entryBarBody >= strongBodyFraction * entryBarRange;
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (bar classification used to gate a stop-tightening decision)

complexity.reason: single-bar body/range arithmetic, but the bar is located dynamically via BarsSinceEntry() rather than a fixed lag

notes: Brooks contrasts this with a doji entry bar (a one-bar trading range), which should NOT trigger tightening.
strongBodyFraction=0.6 is a reading of 'strong'; Brooks gives no number here.

candidates.name: TightenStopToEntryBarIfStrong
candidates.quote: The initial price action stop for most trades is one tick beyond the signal bar until the entry bar closes, when it is tightened to one or two ticks beyond the entry bar if the entry bar is strong.
candidates.description: Once the entry bar closes, if it qualified as a strong trend bar (R29-02), tighten the protective stop from beyond the signal bar to one or two ticks beyond the entry bar's own extreme instead.
candidates.pseudocode: entryBarLow = low[ctx.BarsSinceEntry()]; exitLongStop = ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && isEntryBarStrongTrendBar[0] && ctx.BarsSinceEntry() >= 1 && low[0] <= entryBarLow - tightenOffsetTicks * tick;
candidates.book_order_type: protective sell stop moved to one or two ticks below the entry bar's low

complexity.reason: same dynamic-offset bar lookup as R29-01/R29-02, plus a dependency on the strong-trend-bar classification

notes: Replaces R29-01 once BarsSinceEntry()>=1 and the entry bar qualifies as strong; if the entry bar is a doji instead, R29-01 remains in force ('rely on your original stop').

candidates.name: FractionalSignalBarMoneyManagementStop
candidates.quote: in a long off a large bull signal bar, you would place the protective stop about 30 percent of the distance up from the bottom of the signal bar to the entry price.
candidates.description: When the signal bar is unusually tall, use a money-management stop instead of a full signal-bar-extreme stop: place it a fraction of the way up from the signal bar's low toward the entry price (roughly a 70 percent pullback, a couple of ticks beyond the 62 percent Fibonacci retracement).
candidates.pseudocode: signalBarLow = low[ctx.BarsSinceEntry() + 1]; stopPrice = signalBarLow + stopFraction * (ctx.EntryPrice() - signalBarLow); exitLongStop = ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && low[0] <= stopPrice;
candidates.book_order_type: protective sell stop placed a fraction of the way up from the signal bar's low toward the entry price

complexity.reason: same dynamic bar lookup as R29-01, plus a linear interpolation between the signal bar low and the entry price

notes: Alternative to R29-01 specifically for signal bars too tall to risk the full range; Brooks frames the fraction as roughly the complement of a 62% Fibonacci retracement.

candidates.name: SwingLowTrailingStop
candidates.quote: Since a bull trend is a series of higher highs and higher lows, it is reasonable to move the protective stop to below the most recent swing low after the market makes a new swing high. This is called a trailing stop.
candidates.description: In a trend, once the market makes a new swing high (long) / swing low (short), move the protective stop to one tick beyond the most recent confirmed swing low / high.
candidates.book_order_type: protective sell stop trailed to one tick below the most recent swing low

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection to identify both the triggering new swing high and the most recent confirmed swing low used for the stop level

notes: The chapter's headline trailing-stop technique, walked through bar-by-bar in Figures 29.2 and 29.4.
Distinct from the corpus's dollar-based TrailingStop/AtrTrailingStop, which use profit peaks, not chart swing points.

candidates.name: BreakevenStopAfterHalfwayToTarget
candidates.quote: Once a swing trade reaches about halfway to the profit target, many traders will move their protective stop to break even.
candidates.description: Once the position's peak open profit has reached at least half of the trader's profit target, move the protective stop to breakeven (the entry price); exit if price then returns to breakeven.
candidates.pseudocode: reachedHalfwayToTarget = ctx.MaxPositionProfit() >= 0.5 * profitTargetDollars; exitLong = ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && reachedHalfwayToTarget && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() <= breakevenBandDollars;
candidates.book_order_type: protective stop moved to the entry price (breakeven)

complexity.reason: needs peak-profit tracking (MaxPositionProfit, already used by the corpus's ProfitProtector family) gated by a separately defined dollar profit target

notes: Mechanically close to ProfitProtector (peak profit gives back a fraction), but the gate here is 'reached half of a fixed target' rather than 'reached a fixed floor', and the giveback is to full breakeven rather than a partial fraction.

candidates.name: StopBeyondLowestSinceEntry
candidates.quote: You also should adjust your protective stop at this point to one tick beyond that pullback, so you are now risking 12 ticks.
candidates.description: Ratchet the protective stop to one tick beyond the worst (lowest, for a long) price the market has reached since entry, once that low has held and price has resumed moving in the trade's favor.
candidates.pseudocode: worstPriceSinceEntry = lowest(low, ctx.BarsSinceEntry() + 1)[0]; exitLongStop = ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && low[0] <= worstPriceSinceEntry - ratchetOffsetTicks * tick;
candidates.book_order_type: protective sell stop moved to one tick below the lowest low reached since entry

complexity.reason: a min/max window loop whose window length is the position's own age (BarsSinceEntry()) rather than a fixed constant

notes: Distinct from R29-05 (swing-pivot based): this uses the raw running extreme of the trade itself with no pivot detection, matching the numeric example Brooks walks through (an 11-tick pullback becomes a 12-tick stop).

candidates.name: StopBeyondAverageDailyRangeFraction
candidates.quote: Some traders will consider that the trend is still in effect unless the market falls more than between 50 to 75 percent of the average daily range.
candidates.description: Use a money-management stop sized as a fraction of the instrument's average daily range, rather than a fixed tick count or the signal-bar extreme.
candidates.book_order_type: money-management stop sized as a fraction of the average daily range

complexity.reason: needs a design decision on computing a session/daily range aggregate from the strategy's own bar series, which the engine does not currently expose

el_words_needed: AvgTrueRange (daily) or a new daily-range aggregate, not currently in the register

candidates.name: ProfitTargetEqualsPriorAdverseExcursion
candidates.quote: the market will rally enough to equal the size of the stop that it required you to have to stay in the trade... Now increase your profit target to one or two ticks less than the risk, or 11 ticks.
candidates.description: Set (or raise) the profit target to just under the maximum adverse excursion the trade has already survived, on the premise that the market typically rallies back at least as far as it first moved against the position.
candidates.pseudocode:
// needs the running trough of open profit since entry, the mirror of the already-used MaxPositionProfit peak tracker
worstOpenProfitSinceEntry = ctx.MinPositionProfit(); requiredRiskDollars = -worstOpenProfitSinceEntry; profitTargetDollars = requiredRiskDollars - targetSlackDollars; exitLong = ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() >= profitTargetDollars;
candidates.book_order_type: profit-taking limit order placed one or two ticks less than the worst adverse excursion already survived

complexity.reason: conceptually the mirror of the corpus's MaxPositionProfit peak tracker; just needs an equivalent trough (MinPositionProfit) primitive registered

notes: Unusually precise for this book: Brooks states it almost as a mechanical rule.

candidates.name: ExitOnCloseOfTrendBarNearDevelopingRangeTop
candidates.quote: it makes more sense to exit on the close of a bull trend bar within the next several bars, so that they would be taking profits near the top of the developing trading range rather than below the bottom.
candidates.description: Once a breakout appears to be stalling into a new (second) trading range, exit on the close of any trend bar in the trade's favor within the next several bars instead of continuing to trail the stop below the pullback low.
candidates.book_order_type: exit at the market (or a limit at the close) on the next qualifying trend bar

complexity.reason: the trend-bar test itself is trivial, but recognizing that the breakout is failing to extend and a second trading range is forming is a design decision this chapter does not define mechanically

candidates.name: PartialProfitNearRangeHighOnRangeTransition
candidates.quote: Once the market finally begins to enter a trading range, traders should look to take at least partial profits around the high of the range, rather than relying on their trailing stops.
candidates.description: Once price/context suggests the market is transitioning from a trend into a trading range, take partial profits near the range high rather than continuing to rely on a trailing stop.
candidates.book_order_type: limit order to take partial profits near the developing range high

complexity.reason: two independent open design questions: multi-unit/partial exits, which the engine does not model, and mechanical trading-range-transition detection

notes: Kept per the mining brief's instruction to record scaling-out candidates even though the engine only models a single all-or-nothing position.

candidates.name: ReverseOnFailedPatternStopOut
candidates.quote: When a protective stop is hit before making a scalper's profit, you were trapped into a bad trade, so reversing on the stop is occasionally a good strategy... a failed low 2 short is a good reversal into a long trade... However, a stop run in a tight trading range is not a reversal.
candidates.description: After being stopped out, permit an immediate reversal entry in the opposite direction only when the stop-out itself completes a recognizable failed pattern (e.g., a failed low 2) in a trending context, not merely a stop run inside a tight trading range.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (gates whether the opposite-direction signal may be taken immediately after a stop-out)

complexity.reason: requires classifying the just-stopped-out pattern and its trend context as reversal-worthy, which this chapter does not reduce to a bar-level test

notes: Related to the corpus's FlatOrOpenLossExceeds (permits a reversal once open loss exceeds X dollars, before the stop is even hit); this is the after-the-stop-out version and is explicitly context-gated by Brooks ('depends on context'), not unconditional.

candidates.name: AddOnBelowDojiSignalBar
candidates.quote: experienced traders can consider adding on at a tick or two below a small doji entry bar in a possible new bull trend... relying on the initial stop location for the stop on the added contracts.
candidates.description: Add a second unit to an existing long at a tick or two below a small doji entry bar (effectively buying below what would otherwise be a low 1 short signal bar), using the same initial stop as the first unit.
candidates.book_order_type: buy limit (or stop) a tick or two below the doji entry bar's low, added to an existing long

complexity.reason: multi-unit/pyramided positions with independently tracked stops are not modeled by the engine

notes: Per the mining brief: scaling-in candidates are recorded even though they need multi-unit positions the engine does not support.

candidates.name: DelayStopTighteningUntilProfitThreshold
candidates.quote: The stop was above the signal bar, and you should not tighten to above the high of the most recent bar until after the market had moved about four ticks in your direction or until the market had a reasonably strong bear body.
candidates.description: Do not begin tightening the bar-by-bar trailing stop until open profit has reached a minimum threshold (or a bar with a sufficiently strong body has formed in the trade's favor); before that, keep the wider initial/signal-bar stop.
candidates.pseudocode: profitThresholdReached = ctx.OpenPositionProfit() >= armTightenProfitDollars; allowStopTightening = profitThresholdReached || strongBodyInTradeDirection[0];
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (gates when other tightening rules, e.g. R29-03/R29-05, are allowed to take effect)

complexity.reason: a simple profit-threshold gate layered on top of already-defined tightening rules

notes: Modifies R29-03/R29-05: without this gate, a stop could tighten too early on a single strong-looking bar not yet backed by real profit.

candidates.name: AdaptiveStopFloorFromFirstTradeMAE
candidates.quote: After the market turned down on bar 2, they could have calculated that the market went eight ticks against them before it went their way. That meant that the minimum initial protective stop that they would have had to use to stay in the trade was nine ticks, and they would have remembered that for the rest of the day.
candidates.description: Use the maximum adverse excursion of the session's first trade (the number of ticks the market moved against the position before turning) as a floor on the stop size for all subsequent trades that session.
candidates.book_order_type: money-management stop no smaller than the day's first trade's maximum adverse excursion plus one tick

complexity.reason: requires tracking and persisting a per-session statistic (the first trade's MAE) across subsequent, independent trades -- a session-state design decision the engine does not currently expose

candidates.name: KeepOriginalStopOnCountertrendEntryBarReversal
candidates.quote: if you were buying a reversal up in a strong bear trend, you should usually exit if the market falls below that bear [entry] bar... However, if the entry bar becomes a bear reversal bar [during a with-trend pullback buy], you should usually just keep your protective stop below the signal bar.
candidates.description: When the entry bar closes opposite to the trade direction, whether to keep the wider signal-bar stop (R29-01) or exit at the entry bar's extreme instead depends on the strength/direction of the surrounding trend: a countertrend long entered against a strong bear trend should exit on an adverse entry bar, while a with-trend pullback long can usually keep the original signal-bar stop.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context gate on whether to exit at the entry bar's extreme instead of the signal bar's)

complexity.reason: depends on a 'strong trend' / 'with-trend vs countertrend' context classification this chapter assumes but does not define mechanically

candidates.name: WideStopSizedToBreakoutRun
candidates.quote: Traders can use wide stops when they are fading breakouts in stairs patterns or on trending trading range days... a trader might fade the breakout and risk about five points to make five points, expecting a test of the breakout.
candidates.description: When fading (entering countertrend against) a breakout, size the protective stop to roughly the length of the breakout move already made, since the trade is a bet on a retracement of that move.
candidates.book_order_type: protective stop placed a distance beyond entry equal to (a fraction of) the breakout run being faded

complexity.reason: needs identification of the breakout's start point and extreme (a swing/leg measurement), not just a fixed-length lookback

rejected.quote: Just cut your position size in half or down to a quarter and place the order.
rejected.reason: position-sizing decision, not a bar-level entry/exit test

rejected.quote: this was evident on the 1 minute chart, not shown... Rely on your stop and ignore the 1 minute chart.
rejected.reason: needs bar data from a finer timeframe than the strategy's own chart

rejected.quote: In a big market, there might be a hundred institutions actively trading, each contributing about 1 percent of the total volume... Institutions could care less about us and are not out there running our stops.
rejected.reason: order-flow/market-microstructure commentary, not data the engine can observe from OHLCV bars

rejected.quote: If you are very confident in the reversal because of a large, strong reversal bar and a confluence of other factors, you can use a stop beyond that large signal bar...
rejected.reason: pure discretion ('confluence of other factors') with no bar-level test

chapter_summary: This chapter is Brooks's core treatment of protective and trailing stops: the baseline is one tick beyond the signal bar, tightened to the entry bar once it closes strong (R29-01..R29-03), with several alternative money-management sizings (a fraction of the signal bar's height, a fraction of the average daily range) and several stop-management techniques layered on top (swing-low trailing, ratcheting to the trade's own worst excursion, breakeven after halfway to target, delaying tightening until profit is real). It also raises two chapter-spanning themes the mining brief flags explicitly: scaling in/adding on (R29-13, and touched again by the wide-stop-and-scale-in friend anecdote) and reversing into the opposite trade after a stop-out (R29-12), both of which need engine features (multi-unit positions, session-persistent state) beyond what StrategyGeneratorBE currently models, so they are recorded at 'research' complexity. Most of the chapter's long chart walkthroughs (bar 1, bar 3, bar 5, etc.) are worked examples of the same handful of general rules above rather than new mechanical statements, so they were not mined as separate candidates.
